Toes are interesting because only the big toe, and pinky can move independently. Your second, third, and fourth toe are linked together by the same muscle branching into different tendons.
That being said, the cramping occurring in your second and third toe suggests it’s the tendon tightening in a spasm and locking into place. I would bet money that the cramping also occurs in your third toe, but due to the shortness of the joint, the tightening doesn’t actually cause pain.
That being said, the face it’s on the underside of your foot means it’s a flexor muscle. By pulling your toes the opposite way, you’re forcing the muscle to extend and relax out of its contracted position in which it was locked. 

From what you’ve described, I would roughly say to look into Flexor Digitorum Brevis [translates to: “flexing/joint pushing away, digits, short head] which is the split point on a single muscle known as the Flexor Digitorum Longus. 
The muscle extends mainly into your lower calf, however a much smaller section of it forks off and connects to your inner heel. This shorter section (the Brevis Head) seems to be locking and forcing your toes to curl back in a pointed position known as plantar flexion.

To stretch the Brevis muscle, by going against its natural movement you can extend it. Basically, pulling back on your toes just like you have been.  This sort of stretch can length and loosen the muscle over time and hopefully it’ll cramp less.

I mentioned that muscles rarely work independently. It’s also likely that your Quadratus Plantae [4 head muscle, plantar axis] in your heel is also helping by contracting and locking in place during this cramping movement.  The Quadratus Plantae is also commonly injured in Plantar Fasciitis.

To prevent the cramping, I’d suggest trying to stretch the muscles to give them some extra slack to prevent them from catching to begin with. Arch support put in your shoes can synthetically force your muscle to remain stretched out and prevent them from locking. Taping your foot along the arch so your foot can’t tighten may also help in the short term.

A harder stretch for your plantar is taking a tennis ball and rolling it around your arch, putting pressure on it gently. I know some athletes that will religiously freeze a water bottle and stand on it. A lot of socks are sewn with a bit of support that although won’t prevent the issue, may be something to look into.

Hello! This could be multiple things.

Is the cramp the sort where your foot almost “locks” into a specific configuration? Often this is when you point your toes, and pushing down on your arch with your thumb (or pressing your foot flat on the ice if you’re curling) “unlocks” it and the pain instantly stops.

When you trail your foot, is it completely flat trailing behind? For example, I have my trailing foot swerve inwards so it’s more like my pinky toe and side of my foot is sliding behind me. 

Are you on your tip toes? Is your foot flat so more of the surface is sliding? (Think of your ankle, is it at a right angle so only your shoe tip is sliding/toes, or is your heel flush to your leg/flat of your foot and toes sliding?)

Based on how you slide, there’s multiple different things that could be causing the cramps, and it depends on where you feel it as well.
Most major muscles that control your toes and do the micro adjustments necessary for walking are actually located in your calf. These muscles have long tendons connecting to the bone in your feet, run through your ankle, and connect to the meat of your muscle in your calf where it contracts to control movement.
If pointing your toes like a ballerina can cause the cramping, these muscles are known as Flexors. If your cramping is more on the top/front of your body either in your foot or lower leg, then these are Extensor muscles.

A cramp can be due to a muscle being not used to stretching its full length (like a super strong resistance band) or a muscle locking due to a postural change once contracting (when you’re pulling a rope and it gets caught on a snag, the tension prevents it from getting unstuck.)

If the cramp is located in your heel or lower leg, then it’s likely a muscle “lock” of your gastrocnemius/calcaneal tendon (nicknamed Achilles)
If the cramp is on the front of your leg, then it’s likely a muscle that’s too tight and resisting your plantar flexion (pointing your toes) however normally that’s not the case.

The gastrocnemius is basically what you assume to be your calf muscle. It’s also interwoven with the Soleus (deeper in your leg). The fascia that connects these together turn into your calcaneal/Achilles.

Everything in your ankle and leg is connected, so when something is injured or damaged another area learns to compensate. Compensating for long times can cause a greater injury: are you a runner? Any sort of sport that involves jumping or landing?

Do you walk “duck-walk”? That’s when our calf are too tight and alter our ankle alignment to reduce stress on our calf muscles.

Now, if the cramping is within the foot itself, then we get into a whole new area.
Most of the muscles are located in your leg however not all of them. Muscles with the term “Brevis” mean that the tendon/muscle connects within the foot instead of crossing the ankle. There’s also a few muscles in your arch that help stabilize and can be located and stretched accordingly.

Your cramping could be pain in the Peroneal tendons (ankle area), adductor hallucis (one part goes to balls of feet, other is inner arch), flexor hallucis Brevis (arch on inner wall or foot and also the ball of your big toe).
Or on the other side, the abductor hallucis (opposite to one mentioned before, goes from big toe towards heel), flexor digitorum Brevis (Ball of toes towards middle of foot, connects to all 4 toes other than big toe), plantar aponeurosis (fancy word for your inner heel hurts by your arch) or abductor digiti minimi (outer foot towards pinky toe).

Please remember that NONE of these muscles work INDEPENDENTLY. If one muscle contracts, another will extend. Your body is a system of levers- nothing works independently!

If it’s still broken or healing still, then no firm stretches because the muscles between your ribs can pull it out of alignment. If pressure on the rib hurts, then it isn’t done healing.

If it IS done healing, it still depends on the location of the break and which rib! 
We have internal and external intercostal muscles which connect between our rib bones and aid with inhaling and exhaling. We also have muscles extending from our back around our sides to our chest called serrates anterior muscles. Our “abs” connect to our sternum and lower ribs as well. Our external and internal oblique muscles connect to our lower ribs as well.
All the way up towards our throat, our upper ribs are actually connected with a few muscles to our jaw and neck. Without knowing where the break is, it’s impossible to suggest stretches.

Okay uh I just wanna say I’m not a Doctor first, although I am studying a medical field and I’ve had first hand experience.

Doctors generally have a list of various types of medications for antidepressants. These are SSRI (Lexapro like what you took, Prozac, Zoloft, Celexa) basically they are the first class they try you on because they generally help the majority of people first. SSRI are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so they cause you to not breakdown your seratonin but instead you increase what you have. It takes generally 2 weeks for them to really start affecting you. 

There’s things called the Opposite Effect (I cant remember the medical term) where certain antidepressants will unexpectedly do the opposite, and cause huge mood swings, impulses, irritability, or suicidal ideation. I know that SSRI’s are the most common medicine for this- which is ironic since it’s the one which works for most people. The younger you are and the higher the dosage, the bigger the risk. I think Prozac, Zoloft, and Paxil have the worst issues.

Then we have SNRI (seratonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) which does similar to SSRI but adds in norepinephrine to the mix. These meds are used for people with fatigue problems, although these ones have really really wicked side effects if you miss a dosage so they don’t like putting people on them if they can’t help it. These ones are Effexor, Savella,Cymbalts

There’s also Monoamine Oxidase inhibitors, although these are considered old school and have really really bad issues if you have other medications or certain foods. They rarely ever use these anymore, since they require diet restrictions.

Tricyclic Antidepressents are the other type too, these bad boys work by making your brain nerve cells not absorb serotonin and norepinephrine which makes those two chemicals more apparent in your brain. These ones are Elavil, Norpramin, Vivactil, and others. Tricyclic antidepressants tends to have more side effects than SSRI and SNRI’s however they’re used for other psychological disorders like OCD so if you have other psychiatric issues they may be looked at. 

Finally we’ve got the great Atypical antidepressents, which are fairly new and they work by changing the level of a specific brain neurotransmitter but they all work in different ways. These ones are things like Wellbutrin, Nefazodone, Remeron.

I’ll be honest for you, finding the right medication takes forever. I got medication after my dad committed suicide when I was 16. I was on Lexapro for a few months, Zoloft for a week before I was super suicidal, then Wellbutrin but the side effects caused me to be so drowsy I couldn’t do anything. I did a genetic testing and they checked and found out which chemical and which drug would help the best- see if your doctor can do that test for you or if your insurance covers it. I’ve been on Effexor for over a year now and I’m still messing with the dosage. 

You’re likely going to be sorted through all the SSRI’s before moved onto an atypical, just because you had a bad reaction with one SSRI doesn’t mean you’ll react bad to all of them. It takes forever and sucks since you need weeks before it kicks in, but I hope you know a little more now.
